title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 2: Incomplete Victory
keywords: the mansion owners of Forbes Park
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's May 13, 2007 Inquirer column calling the Court's Bantay Republic v. Comelec ruling (which ordered the disclosure of party-list nominees' names) only an 'incomplete victory,' because it 'summarily denied' the bid to disqualify 31 party-list candidates

His critique that the Court answered only the narrow 'simultaneous'-timing argument and 'totally ignored' whether the 31 respondents met the Court's own guidelines and RA 7941 -- never reaching whether they truly belonged to the 'marginalized and underrepresented sectors' or were government-funded

The contrasting precedent he prefers -- Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (2001), which held the party-list system reserved for the marginalized (no government 'adjunct'), remanded the case for a factual qualifications check, and barred proclamations until the Court ruled -- reaffirmed by a 12-1 vote in 2003 (CJP among the majority)

His warning that, by not remanding or holding the proclamations, the Court risked letting the Comelec 'simply proclaim the winners' and render the qualifications issue academic -- 'a cop-out... an unmitigated desecration of the party-list system and a muscular stomp on the poor and the weak'
sub_topics: The half-won battle: Bantay Republic v. Comelec (May 4, 2007) was 'greeted with jubilation' for ordering the Comelec to 'immediately disclose and release the names of the nominees' so voters could be 'more informed' -- but 'the battle may have been only half-won'

What the Court refused: it 'summarily denied' Bantay Republic's (BA-RA 7941's) petition to disqualify 31 party-list candidates, answering only that 'nowhere in RA 7941' is the nominee's qualification required to be determined 'simultaneously' with the organization's accreditation

The ignored issue: the decision 'totally ignored the alleged failure of the 31 respondents' to comply with the Court's guidelines and RA 7941, never discussing whether they 'truly belonged to the marginalized and underrepresented sectors' or 'were funded by the government'

The Ang Bagong Bayani precedent (2001): challenging the Comelec's accreditation of 154 organizations, the Court (voting 9-5) held that only those belonging to 'marginalized and underrepresented sectors' qualified, and that a party 'must not be an adjunct of, or... funded or assisted by, the government'

The marginalized doctrine in vivid terms: 'the law crafted to address the peculiar disadvantages of the Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park,' nor by 'bankers, industrialists and sugar planters'

The remand mechanism: the Court remanded for the Comelec to determine factually which of the 154 qualified, issued 'eight guidelines... culled from the law and the Constitution,' and directed the poll body 'to refrain from proclaiming any winner' until the Court acted -- necessary because once congressmen are proclaimed, the Court loses jurisdiction to the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET)

The 2003 reaffirmation: on June 25, 2003 the Court issued a 'definitive resolution' approving the Comelec's reports, reiterating the 'marginalized and underrepresented' doctrine by a 12-1 vote (Vitug dissenting; CJP among the majority and the original ponente)

The contrast and the stakes: against that careful approach, Bantay Republic gave petitioners 'the short shrift'; CJP argues it would have been 'more judicious to remand the cases and to hold the proclamations until the questions on the qualifications of the 31 respondents are settled,' lest the Comelec proclaim winners and render the qualifications issue 'academic' -- 'a cop-out... an unmitigated desecration of the party-list system and a muscular stomp on the poor and the weak'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's May 13, 2007 Inquirer column, calls the Court's Bantay Republic v. Comelec ruling only an 'incomplete victory.' The decision was 'greeted with jubilation' for ordering the Comelec to 'immediately disclose and release the names of the nominees' so voters could be 'more informed' -- but, he writes, 'the battle may have been only half-won,' because the Court 'summarily denied' the bid to disqualify 31 party-list candidates. It answered only the narrow argument that RA 7941 nowhere requires a nominee's qualification to be determined 'simultaneously' with the organization's accreditation, and 'totally ignored' whether the 31 respondents met the Court's own guidelines and the law -- never reaching whether they 'truly belonged to the marginalized and underrepresented sectors' or were government-funded. He contrasts this with Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (2001), where the Court (9-5) held the party-list system reserved for the marginalized -- a party 'must not be an adjunct of, or... funded or assisted by, the government' -- and famously said a law for 'the Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park.' That case remanded the matter for a factual qualifications check, issued eight guidelines, and barred proclamations until the Court ruled (crucial because, once party-list congressmen are proclaimed, jurisdiction passes to the HRET), and was reaffirmed 12-1 in 2003. Against that careful approach, Bantay Republic gave petitioners 'the short shrift'; CJP argues the Court should have remanded and held the proclamations until the 31 respondents' qualifications were settled, lest the Comelec 'simply proclaim the winners' and render the issue 'academic' -- 'a cop-out... an unmitigated desecration of the party-list system and a muscular stomp on the poor and the weak.'
